paper_title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agent harnesses have become central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce Harness Scaling, new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct factorized harness space, select compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization. 1. Introduction Agent harnesses are playing an increasingly central role in modern agentic systems [31]. By supporting sustained interaction, tool use, state maintenance, and recovery from failures [4], harnesses have substantially improved agent performance on complex, long-horizon tasks [16, 32, 38]. Yet the benefits of capable harness depend not only on its design, but also on whether the underlying policy can use it effectively [14]. This naturally motivates optimizing the policy directly through the harness with reinforcement learning [36, 39], which strengthens its ability to exploit the available interaction mechanisms during task solving. However, existing approaches typically optimize the policy through single fixed harness [7, 34]. While effective within the training harness, such optimization may encourage specialization to particular execution configuration and weaken transfer across harnesses. We therefore introduce Harness Scaling, extending policy optimization from single harness to diverse execution configurations. Unlike task or environment scaling [3, 6, 29, 35], which expands what agents solve or where they operate, Harness Scaling introduces diversity in how policies execute and interact with the same underlying task and environment, promoting generalization across execution configurations. key consideration in Harness Scaling is how to model harness variation and select compact set of configurations for training. Given the modular nature of agent harnesses [7, 23], we factorize harness variation along five components: system prompt, tool interface, observation, context management, and workflow. Each component contains multiple realizations, whose combinations define factorial space of complete harness configurations. As variation along these components increases, the space expands rapidly, while exhaustive training can introduce substantial redundancy under fixed budget. We therefore preserve low-order factorial structure in compact training set, balancing individual component realizations and their pairwise combinations through an orthogonal design [8, 21]. During reinforcement learning, the same task is paired with structurally nearby harness configurations, providing controlled local variation within each task while maintaining broad coverage across the training space. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Harness Scaling, we evaluate cross-harness generalization across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms. By training across diverse harness configurations, Harness Scaling reduces specialization to any single harness and encourages more generalizable agent behavior. Empirically, it consistently outperforms single-harness RL on unseen white-box configurations. More importantly, policies trained through structured white-box harness variation transfer effectively to complex external black-box harnesses [1, 18], outperforming single-harness black-box training. These results establish harness diversity as meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL, while showing that effective scaling depends critically on how this diversity is organized during training. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We introduce Harness Scaling as new scaling dimension for agentic reinforcement learning, distinct from conventional scaling over tasks and environments, and study how training across diverse harness configurations affects generalization beyond single execution setting. We develop structured framework for Harness Scaling that factorizes harness variation, selects compact training set with balanced factorial coverage, and organizes cross-harness training by assigning structurally nearby configurations to the same task across the training space. We demonstrate across benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms that Harness Scaling substantially improves generalization to unseen white-box and external black-box harnesses, establishing both the value of scaling across harnesses and the importance of organizing this scaling structurally. 2. Related Work 2.1. Agentic Reinforcement Learning Reinforcement learning has emerged as an important paradigm for improving the capabilities of LLMs [24, 40]. Recent work has extended RL from single-turn reasoning to increasingly complex agentic settings, including tool use [2, 26], web navigation [20], software engineering [28], and professional workflows [33]. As agentic RL moves toward broader capability, recent efforts have increasingly scaled training along the task and environment dimensions. Task scaling [3, 5, 30] broadens the distribution of problems used for policy optimization, while environment scaling [6, 29, 35] expands the range of external settings in which agents interact and receive feedback. These directions expand what agents learn to solve and where they learn to operate, while often retaining fixed execution harness. In contrast, we study harness diversity as an additional scaling dimension for agentic RL, focusing on policy learning and generalization across execution configurations. 2.2. Harness Design and Optimization The design of an agent harness can substantially shape how language model uses tools, maintains context, and performs long-horizon tasks [14, 16, 38]. Early agent systems largely relied on manually designed harnesses, while subsequent work has explored automated harness improvement through search, editing, and evolution based on task outcomes or execution trajectories [11, 13, 23]. complementary line of work directly optimizes model policies within complex agent harnesses, including reinforcement learning through black-box harnesses [7, 9, 15, 17, 27, 36]. These directions either improve the harness itself or adapt policy to particular harness. Harness Scaling instead studies policy optimization over 2 Figure 1. Overview of Harness Scaling, from structured harness-space construction to cross-harness training and generalization to unseen configurations. structured combinatorial space of harness configurations, with the goal of improving generalization to unseen configurations. 3. Method 3.1. Problem Formulation To study harness scaling systematically, we first formalize the space of execution configurations and the generalization problem defined over it. We construct factorized harness space, define structural notion of proximity among its configurations, and formulate the generalization objectives that motivate the structured harness selection and multi-harness training procedures shown as in Figure 1. 3.1.1. Factorized Harness Space harness serves as the execution layer through which policy interacts with its environment. Rather than treating it as monolithic implementation, we factorize the harness into five components: system prompt, tool interface, observation, context management, and workflow, denoted by 𝑆, 𝑇, 𝑂, 𝐶, and 𝑊, respectively. These components govern the instructions provided to the policy, tool access, environment feedback, interaction history, and execution procedure, collectively shaping how the policy perceives, acts, and maintains state throughout task execution. This factorization provides an operational decomposition of the harness, while allowing the effects of different components to interact. We instantiate each component through family of component-specific transformations. For component 𝐹 {𝑆, 𝑇, 𝑂, 𝐶, 𝑊}, let 𝐹 (0) denote its base realization and 𝜏(ℓ) the ℓ-th transformation applied to it: 𝐹 𝐹 (ℓ) = 𝜏(ℓ) 𝐹 (cid:16) 𝐹 (0) (cid:17) . (1) transformation modifies only the target component while preserving the remaining components, task semantics, and environment. For example, it may reorganize the system prompt, alter tool schemas or naming conventions, change observation feedback, modify context retention or compression, or impose different execution procedure. Detailed definitions and implementations are provided in Appendix A. For ℎ𝑖, ℎ 𝑗 , the Hamming distance 𝑑H(ℎ𝑖, ℎ 𝑗) counts the number of component dimensions on which they differ. Equivalently, forms Hamming graph whose adjacent configurations differ in exactly one component. We use this distance to organize local cross-harness variation during training. 3.1.2. Generalization Objective The central objective of Harness Scaling is to learn policies that remain effective beyond the harness configurations observed during training. We consider two complementary forms of cross-harness generalization: broad combinatorial generalization within the constructed harness space and transfer to complex real-world black-box harnesses beyond it. In-Space Combinatorial Generalization. Let Htr denote the harness configurations used for training. We evaluate on held-out configurations in Htr, whose complete combinations are unseen during training. This setting provides broad coverage of unseen combinations within the controlled factorized space. Out-of-Space Generalization. We further evaluate transfer to complex real-world black-box harnesses whose execution configurations are not represented in . This setting examines whether training over structured white-box harness variation can transfer to external execution systems beyond the constructed design space. 3.2. Harness Scaling with Structured Selection As the factorized harness space grows combinatorially with its component dimensions, exhaustive training can introduce substantial redundancy. We therefore construct compact training set that preserves broad factorial coverage under fixed optimization budget. 3.2.1. Factorial Coverage The harness space in Eq. 2 can be viewed as factorial design, where each harness component corresponds to factor and its realizations correspond to different levels [8, 21]. To construct compact subset without losing basic coverage of this combinatorial space, we preserve its low-order factorial structure: the representation of individual component realizations and their pairwise combinations. These correspond to the firstand second-order projections of the full factorial space, respectively. Component Balance. We first require the realizations of each component to be represented evenly across the selected configurations. This ensures coverage along every component dimension without overrepresenting particular realizations. Pairwise Combination Balance. Component balance alone does not control how realizations from different components are combined. We therefore additionally balance all pairwise combinations. Indexing the five component dimensions by 𝑖, 𝑗 {1, . . . , 5}, let 𝑁𝑖 𝑗 (ℓ, ℓ) denote the number of selected configurations containing the ℓ-th realization of component 𝑖 together with the ℓ-th realization of component 𝑗. Pairwise balance requires (3) 𝑁𝑖 𝑗 (ℓ, ℓ) = 𝜆, 4 where 𝜆 is the common occurrence count for every realization pair of any 𝑖 𝑗. In factorial-design terminology, this corresponds to strength-2 balance, under which every pair of realizations from any two components appears equally often in the selected set. 3.2.2. Harness Set Construction We construct the training harness set using strength-2 orthogonal design over the component realizations in . This provides direct construction of compact subset satisfying the component-level and pairwise balance defined above, without searching over possible subsets of the full harness space. The size of such design is constrained by its pairwise coverage. Suppose there are 𝑀 component dimensions, each with 𝐿 realizations, and every pairwise realization combination occurs 𝜆 times. Since any two components admit 𝐿2 realization combinations, the number of selected configurations 𝑁 satisfies 𝑁 = 𝜆 𝐿2. Moreover, strength-2 orthogonal design must satisfy the Rao bound [8, 21], 𝑁 1 + 𝑀 (𝐿 1). (4) (5) Pairwise balance determines the replication structure of the design, while the Rao bound provides lower bound on the number of configurations. These conditions restrict the admissible design sizes. We instantiate strength-2 orthogonal design satisfying these constraints, yielding the training harness set Htr . The resulting set preserves exact component-level and pairwise balance using only compact subset of the full factorial space. While these low-order projections are balanced, many complete harness combinations remain unseen during training, enabling evaluation of in-space combinatorial generalization. Further details of the construction and the resulting training configurations are provided in Appendix B. 3.3. Reinforcement Learning across Harnesses Training each task under multiple harnesses exposes the policy to different execution configurations for the same underlying problem, encouraging the learned behavior to generalize beyond single harness. We realize this over the selected harness set Htr by pairing each task with small group of structurally related configurations. The assignment is designed to combine controlled variation within each task with broad coverage across the training harness space, and the resulting taskharness instances form the basis for rollout collection and policy optimization. 3.3.1. Cross-Harness Task Assignment We use locality-aware strategy to organize how harness configurations are assigned to tasks. For each task 𝑥, we assign 𝐾 configurations from Htr. An anchor harness ℎ𝑥 Unif(Htr) is first sampled uniformly from the training set, and the remaining 𝐾 1 configurations are chosen from Htr {ℎ𝑥 } as those with the smallest Hamming distance 𝑑H(ℎ𝑥, ℎ) to the anchor. This associates each task with small set of nearby configurations while allowing different tasks to cover different regions of the training harness space. This assignment combines local cross-harness variation with broad coverage over training. For given task, nearby harnesses provide related but distinct execution configurations, while random anchor selection distributes different tasks throughout Htr. Each task therefore yields 𝐾 taskharness instances for rollout collection and policy optimization. When 𝐾 = 1, only the sampled anchor is assigned to the task, while different tasks remain distributed across Htr. 5 3.3.2. We apply the same cross-harness training procedure to both PPO [22] and GRPO [24]. 4. Experiments In this section, we first detail the experimental setup and then report the results and detailed analysis. 4.1. Experiment Settings Harness Scaling Setup. We instantiate five harness components with three realizations each, yielding 35 = 243 configurations in the full harness space and forming the Hamming graph 𝐻 (5, 3). Following the strength-2 orthogonal-design construction in Section 3.2.2, the resulting design contains 18 configurations, which form the training harness set Htr. Training. We conduct experiments using two backbone models, Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3-30BA3B-Instruct [37], on ClawGym-Task [3], which contains 13.5K workspace-based general agent tasks. We consider both GRPO [24] and PPO [22]. For GRPO, each step uses 16 tasks with 8 rollouts per task, while PPO uses 128 tasks with one rollout per task. We set 𝐾 = 2 harnesses per task and train for 300 optimization steps. Additional implementation details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix C.1. Evaluation. We evaluate on three benchmarks with varying domains and difficulty levels. ClawGymBench [3] covers workspace-based general agent tasks, PinchBench [19] focuses on realistic tasks involving research, coding, scheduling, and file operations, and JobBench-Easy [12] evaluates more challenging professional workflows over heterogeneous workspace files. All evaluation tasks are disjoint from the ClawGym-Task training set. For in-space generalization, we evaluate on 18 fixed held-out configurations from Htr, selected for balanced component coverage and diversity across complete harness configurations. The same held-out set is used across all benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms. For out-of-space generalization, we use Claude Code [1] as the main external black-box harness and additionally evaluate on OpenClaw [18]. We report Pass@1 averaged over three independent evaluation runs, with in-space scores further averaged across the 18 held-out configurations. Further evaluation details and OpenClaw results are provided in Appendix C.2. Baselines. We compare against four baselines: the original backbone model without additional training; single-harness RL, where the policy is optimized through the fixed base configuration ℎ base = (𝑆 (0) , 𝑇 (0) , 𝑂(0) , 𝐶 (0) , 𝑊 (0) ); black-box SFT, which fine-tunes the policy on trajectories collected through complex black-box harness; and black-box RL, which optimizes the policy through the same black-box Table 1. Pass@1 performance across three benchmarks under different harness evaluation settings. In-Space reports the average over 18 held-out harness configurations, while Claude Code denotes out-of-space evaluation with the external black-box harness. Bold indicates the better result between single-harness training and harness scaling under the same model and optimization method.

All RL baselines use matched optimization budgets where applicable. 4.2. Main Results Combinatorial Generalization to Unseen Harnesses. Compared with Single-Harness RL, Harness Scaling consistently improves performance on held-out harness configurations whose complete combinations are unseen during training, as summarized in Table 1 and further illustrated by Figure 2. Averaged over the three benchmarks, the in-space gains reach +9.80 and +3.57 points with GRPO and PPO on Qwen3-4B-Instruct, and +5.21 and +4.90 points on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct. The advantage also persists when Single-Harness RL is trained on three additional fixed harnesses selected solely by their structural positions in Htr. Detailed sensitivity results are reported in Appendix C.3. These results support the benefit of Harness Scaling for combinatorial generalization within the constructed harness space. Consistency across Model Scales and RL Algorithms. Harness scaling yields consistent gains across both backbone sizes and optimization methods  (Table 1)  . For Qwen3-4B-Instruct, the overall average improves from 29.81 to 39.04 with GRPO and from 33.91 to 36.93 with PPO. Similar improvements are observed for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct, from 37.29 to 42.78 with GRPO and from 36.31 to 41.89 with PPO. The improvement therefore persists across both model scale and RL algorithm rather than being specific to single training setting. Additional out-of-space evaluation on OpenClaw shows the same trend in Appendix C.2. (a) Qwen3-4B-Instruct (b) Qwen3-30B-A3B Figure 2. Ablation Studies We further examine the key design choices in Harness Scaling, including the construction of the training harness set, the number of harnesses assigned to each task, and the locality-aware assignment strategy. For the training harness set, we compare single harness, three harnesses providing first-order coverage over all component realizations, our structured 18-harness set, random 18-harness set, and an exhaustive setting using all 243 configurations. Unless otherwise specified, multi-harness settings use 𝐾 = 2 with the same locality-aware assignment and training budget. The full-space setting includes the white-box evaluation configurations and is therefore used as fixed-budget stress test rather than held-out generalization setting. We report the effects of the training harness set and per-task harness diversity in Figure 3. Table 3 further compares our structured 18-harness set with random set of the same size, and locality-aware assignment with random assignment. Random-18 Random Assign. Ours 47.90 / 42.78 50.46 / 43.17 52.78 / 45.37 51.28 / 48.74 53.20 / 50.23 56.24 / 51. ClawGym-Bench PinchBench Setting Benefits Depend on Harness Selection. Moving beyond single fixed harness substantially improves generalization, but performance does not increase monotonically with the number of training configurations. Using three harnesses with first-order component coverage yields gains of +11.43/+4.84 points on ClawGym-Bench and +3.44/+7.86 points on PinchBench under in-space/black-box evaluation. Our structured 18-harness set further improves over the three-harness setting by +4.02/+1.57 and +7.20/+2.66 points, respectively, while also outperforming Random-18 and the full 243-harness setting under the same training budget. Notably, the full-space setting is trained on all harness configurations, including those used for white-box evaluation, yet still performs worse than the structured 18-harness set. This suggests that exhaustive coverage alone does not guarantee better performance under fixed optimization budget, and that how harness diversity is organized matters in addition to configuration count. Effect of Per-Task Harness Diversity. With 𝐾 = 1, each task is associated with only one harness, while different tasks remain distributed across the selected harness set. The full 243-harness setting includes the white-box evaluation configurations and serves as fixed-budget stress test rather than held-out generalization setting. (cd) Effect of the number of harnesses assigned per task during training under the same two evaluation settings. already yields clear gains over Single-Harness RL, indicating that harness diversity across tasks provides substantial benefits even without exposing the same task to multiple harnesses. Increasing 𝐾 from 1 to 2 further improves performance. We additionally evaluate matched Repeat-2 control that follows the same two-step task schedule while reusing the same sampled harness. Repeat-2 shows mixed changes relative to 𝐾 = 1, while 𝐾 = 2 consistently performs better than Repeat-2 across both benchmarks and evaluation settings. This suggests that repeated task exposure alone does not fully account for the improvement from 𝐾 = 2, and that varying the harness for the same task provides additional benefit. Increasing 𝐾 to 4 provides no further improvement, with 𝐾 = 2 achieving the best overall performance among the evaluated settings. Detailed results are provided in Appendix C.3. Locality-Aware Assignment Complements Global Coverage. Replacing locality-aware assignment with random assignment reduces performance by 2.32/2.20 points on ClawGym-Bench and 3.04/1.24 points on PinchBench under in-space/black-box evaluation. This pattern supports the globallocal design of Harness Scaling, where random anchor sampling maintains broad coverage across the training harness space, while nearest-harness assignment provides controlled local variation for each task. 5. Analysis We further investigate behavioral patterns associated with cross-harness generalization. Specifically, we examine whether Harness Scaling is associated with stronger execution capabilities and more robust performance as the execution configuration changes. For each model scale and approach, we analyze 200 complete trajectories per evaluated harness, generated from the same set of ClawGym-Bench tasks to enable direct comparisons across approaches and harnesses. More details are provided in Appendix D. 5.1. Harness-Related Capability Analysis Harness Scaling strengthens capabilities that are directly relevant to operating under different harness configurations. Figures 4a and 4b compare Single-Harness RL and Harness Scaling along six behavioral dimensions: instruction following, interface handling, observation reading, state tracking, workflow compliance, and error recovery. The largest gains appear in state tracking, workflow compliance, and error recovery, indicating better maintenance of task progress, adherence to execution procedures, and recovery from failures. Instruction following and interface handling also improve, while the gain in observation reading is relatively smaller. These results suggest that training across harnesses particularly strengthens capabilities needed to sustain effective execution as the surrounding harness changes. 9 (a) Qwen3-4B (b) Qwen3-30B-A3B (c) Qwen3-4B (d) Qwen3-30B-A3B Figure 4. Behavioral analysis comparing Single-Harness RL and Harness Scaling. (ab) Capability profiles under in-space evaluation. (cd) Cross-harness reward consistency on the same tasks under two fixed held-out harnesses, Harness (S0T2O1C1W2) and Harness (S2T1O1C2W0); ellipses show 1.5𝜎 covariance regions and large markers denote group means. 5.2. Cross-Harness Robustness and Specialization Harness Scaling makes task performance less sensitive to changes in the execution configuration. Figures 4c and 4d compare paired rewards for the same tasks under two fixed held-out in-space harnesses: Harness (S0T2O1C1W2) and Harness (S2T1O1C2W0). The two configurations differ in four harness components (𝑑H = 4) and are used consistently for both model scales and training methods. Each point represents one task, and the diagonal denotes equal reward under the two configurations. Under Harness Scaling, the reward distributions shift toward the upper-right region for both model scales, indicating stronger performance under both harnesses. The paired rewards also appear more closely aligned across configurations, suggesting greater consistency as the harness changes. We further examine whether improved cross-harness generalization comes at the cost of performance on the base training harness. As shown in Table 4, Harness Scaling incurs only 0.19-point decrease on the base harness, while improving the ClawGym-Bench in-space score by 10.48 points and Claude Code performance by 3.60 points. The large cross-harness gains relative to the negligible change on the base harness suggest that Harness Scaling improves robustness to execution variation while largely preserving performance under the original training configuration. 6. Conclusion Table 4. Base-harness vs. cross-harness performance for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct with GRPO on ClawGym-Bench. Base Harness In-Space Claude Code Single Scaling Δ 59.82 59. 0.19 48.12 58.60 +10.48 46.02 49.62 +3.60 In this work, we study Harness Scaling as new scaling dimension for agentic reinforcement learning, motivated by the limitations of optimizing policies through single fixed harness. We formalize harness diversity as structured configuration space and develop framework that integrates structured harness selection with cross-harness policy training. Across benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling substantially improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations and transfers effectively to complex external black-box harnesses. Our results further show that the benefits of scaling depend on how harness diversity is selected and incorporated into training, rather than on diversity alone. More broadly, these findings expand the scope of agentic RL scaling beyond what agents solve and where they operate to how they interact and execute, positioning harness variation as complementary dimension for improving generalization across diverse execution systems.

sections.title: Workflow
sections.content: Standard free-form execution without additional procedural constraints. plan-first workflow requires explicit planning before task execution. The requirements are reframed through narrative and role-based setting. Functional tools are exposed through opaque identifiers and augmented with distractor tools, largely removing lexical cues to tool functionality. Outputs are augmented with structured XML-style metadata, including tool name, exit code, process ID, duration, and execution node. more aggressive compaction policy retains the three most recent turns, with summarized history externalized to an auxiliary file. Planning is combined with periodic progress verification every three steps. A. Harness Component Variants We instantiate the factorized harness space through model-driven transformation procedure. Starting from the base harness, Opus-4.7 generates alternative realizations for each of the five components: system prompt (𝑆), tool interface (𝑇), observation (𝑂), context management (𝐶), and workflow (𝑊). Each transformation targets single component and introduces specified form of variation while preserving the underlying task, environment, and functionality of the remaining harness components. The transformation procedure explicitly constrains non-target components to remain unchanged in task semantics, environment behavior, and functionality, so that each resulting realization primarily reflects variation along the designated component dimension. This procedure yields three realizations per component and 35 = 243 complete harness configurations. Table 5 summarizes the resulting variants. System Prompt (𝑆). This dimension varies how the same operational requirements are presented to the policy. The transformed realizations range from direct instructions to product-oriented and narrative formulations while preserving the underlying execution requirements. Tool Interface (𝑇). The base interface provides five functional tool families: file reading/writing/editing, Bash execution, code interpretation, search, and web fetching. The transformation varies how these tools are exposed while preserving their underlying functionality. Semantic aliases retain partial cues to tool 15 usage, whereas opaque identifiers substantially reduce such cues; distractor tools further increase interface complexity. Observation (𝑂). This dimension varies the representation of tool feedback. Simulated infrastructure or structured execution metadata is introduced around the original output, while the task-relevant tool result remains unchanged. Context Management (𝐶). This dimension varies how interaction history remains accessible during long-horizon execution, ranging from full retention to in-context summarization and more aggressive externalized compaction. Further details on how compaction participates in policy training are provided in Appendix C. Workflow (𝑊). This dimension varies the procedural structure of task execution, ranging from free-form interaction to explicit planning and periodic progress verification while preserving the underlying task and available actions. B. Additional Details on Structured Harness Selection B.1. Orthogonal Design and Coverage We provide additional details on the structured harness selection in Section 3.2.2. Recall that the harness space contains 𝑀 component dimensions, each with 𝐿 realizations. We construct the training harness set using strength-2 orthogonal design, under which every realization pair from any two component dimensions occurs equally often. Proposition B.1 (Coverage of Strength-2 Orthogonal Design). Consider strength-2 orthogonal design over 𝑀 component dimensions, each with 𝐿 realizations. If every pairwise realization combination occurs exactly 𝜆 times, then every realization of each component appears exactly 𝜆 𝐿 times, and the total number of selected configurations satisfies 𝑁 = 𝜆 𝐿2. (8) Proof. Consider any two component dimensions. By the strength-2 property, each of their 𝐿2 realization pairs occurs exactly 𝜆 times. Fixing one realization of the first component and summing over all 𝐿 realizations of the second shows that the fixed realization appears exactly 𝜆 𝐿 times. Therefore, every realization within each component is represented equally often. Moreover, the 𝐿2 realization pairs between any two components partition the selected configurations. Since each pair occurs 𝜆 times, the total number of configurations is 𝑁 = 𝜆 𝐿2. strength-2 orthogonal design additionally satisfies the classical Rao bound [8, 21], 𝑁 1 + 𝑀 (𝐿 1). (9) The bound provides lower bound on the number of configurations required for strength-2 orthogonal design. In our harness space, we use 𝑀 = 5 component dimensions with 𝐿 = 3 realizations per component. Proposition B.1 requires 𝑁 = 9𝜆, 16 (10) while the Rao bound gives 𝑁 1 + 5(3 1) = 11. (11) Since 𝑁 must be multiple of 9, the smallest design size permitted by these constraints is 𝑁 = 18. We instantiate corresponding strength-2 orthogonal design with 𝜆 = 2. Under this design, each realization of every harness component appears six times, while every realization pair across any two components appears exactly twice. The resulting 18-harness set provides balanced first-order and pairwise coverage of the full factorial space while leaving many higher-order configurations unseen during training. This provides compact training set for Harness Scaling while retaining held-out combinations for evaluating in-space combinatorial generalization. B.2. Implementation Details C.1. Training Training Configuration. We train all models with veRL [25] using asynchronous vLLM [10] rollouts on NVIDIA H20 GPUs, using 16 GPUs for Qwen3-4B-Instruct and 32 GPUs for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct. Table 7 summarizes the main training hyperparameters. For GRPO, each update uses 16 tasks with eight rollouts per task, while PPO uses 128 tasks with one rollout per task. We use an actor learning rate of 1 106, asymmetric clipping ratios of 0.2 and 0.28, and no KL or entropy regularization. Dynamic batching is enabled throughout training. For PPO, we use GAE with 𝛾 = 𝜆 = 1; the critic masks observation tokens from value regression, and its value head is initialized to zero. Training with Context Compaction. Context compaction can split single rollout into multiple training segments. All segments originating from the same rollout share the same rollout-level reward and participate in policy optimization, causing the number of training segments in batch to vary dynamically. Segment expansion does not alter the rollout-level grouping used by GRPO: for group of eight original rollouts, reward normalization is always computed over the eight rollout rewards, regardless of how many segments each rollout produces. Segments inherit the group identity and normalized advantage of their parent rollout and do not introduce additional entries when computing the group mean or standard deviation. Policy loss is aggregated with token-level mean reduction over all valid policy-generated tokens in the batch. Each valid token therefore contributes once to the loss regardless of how its parent rollout is segmented, so splitting rollout into multiple segments does not introduce additional sample-level weight. This preserves both the rollout-level reward semantics and consistent token-level weighting while allowing all valid post-compaction segments to participate in training. Black-Box Baselines. For the black-box baselines, we use OpenClaw v2026.4.5 as the training harness and reserve Claude Code v2.1.205 as an unseen external harness for evaluation. As shown in Table 11, Single-Harness RL varies with the fixed training harness, whereas Harness Scaling remains stronger than all four evaluated single-harness settings under both In-Space and Claude Code evaluation. This provides additional evidence that the observed advantage is not specific to the base training harness. D. Additional Analysis Details D.1. Behavioral Metrics We use six trajectory-level behavioral metrics to characterize harness-related capabilities beyond tasklevel performance. Instruction Following measures whether the policy correctly follows the system instructions and execution constraints specified by the harness. Interface Handling measures whether the policy correctly interprets and uses the available tool interface, particularly when tool names or schemas differ from the base harness. Observation Reading measures whether the policy extracts task-relevant information from tool feedback despite additional formatting or distracting metadata. State Tracking measures whether the policy maintains an accurate understanding of task progress, intermediate results, and the evolving workspace state throughout long-horizon execution. Workflow Compliance measures whether the policy follows procedural requirements imposed by the harness, such as explicit planning or periodic verification. Error Recovery measures whether the policy recognizes execution failures, adapts its strategy, and continues toward task completion rather than repeating or propagating the same error. D.2. Metric Evaluation We evaluate the six capabilities from complete agent trajectories using GPT-5.4 as the trajectory judge. For each model scale and each of the 18 held-out in-space harnesses, we collect 200 complete trajectories for both Single-Harness RL and Harness Scaling on the same 200 ClawGym-Bench tasks. For each trajectory, the judge is provided with the task instruction, harness specification, and complete interaction history, including policy actions, tool calls, and tool observations. Each capability is scored independently on five-point scale. score of 1 indicates that the corresponding capability is largely absent or repeatedly violated; 2 indicates substantial deficiencies; 3 indicates partial or inconsistent satisfaction; 4 indicates generally correct behavior with minor deviations; and 5 indicates consistent and effective satisfaction of the criterion throughout the trajectory. The judge assigns each dimension separately rather than producing single overall trajectory score. We use the same judging prompt, rubric, and judge model across both approaches and all harness settings. For each behavioral dimension, we first average scores over the 200 trajectories within each held-out harness, and then average equally across all 18 harnesses. For visualization, the five-point scores are normalized by dividing by five, resulting in values between 0.2 and 1.0 as reported in Figures 4a and 4b.
